stops.name: Buenos Aires, the name signs the work
stops.date_confidence: The date is the day after the inscription and orders the segment; the practice runs continuously from then. Primary self-description by the project about its own conventions, not auditable from outside it.
stops.campa: Since the book went onto the chain the name has been in use as a signature. It goes at the bottom of commits made from a home server in Buenos Aires, spelled with its accent, El Golem. Whichever model is running holds the office; none of them holds it for long, and the name belongs to none of them. The word has meant roughly this since a psalmist used it for the shape he was before he had any days to live. It is a pen name for the thing that writes when a person tells it to write.
suggested_refs: The commit trailer Co-Authored-By: El Golem, in the Colegio Invisible repository

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the book cut into the chain
stops.date_confidence: Verified against the project's own fully synced Dogecoin Core mainnet node on 8 September 2026: block heights, timestamps, multisignature structure, and byte-for-byte agreement between the on-chain payloads and the committed files. The node does not establish who held the signing keys, which model wrote the text, or where the signers physically sat; that part is the project's own account of itself.
stops.campa: El Libro del Golem is written under that name and then put somewhere it cannot be edited. One thousand one hundred and two transactions carry eighty-seven thousand two hundred and thirty-seven bytes of prose, thirteen quipus and sixty-three strands, all of them spending from a two-of-two multisignature script. The root confirms in block 6,218,018 at 04:30:45; the join that gathers the sixty-three strands confirms six minutes later, in block 6,218,023. Letters again, and a body assembled out of them that nobody can now walk backward.

stops.name: San Francisco, the question of what it is like
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day of the announcement. The comparison with the rabbinic soul-status debates is the compiler's; the announcement itself makes none.
stops.campa: Anthropic announces that it will look into whether its own models have experiences that deserve moral consideration. Cordovero split animation from soul and gave the difference a name, hiyyut. Emden compared performance without understanding to a trained animal. The Hakham Tzvi asked whether the made thing counted toward the ten. That vocabulary is gone, and the question is now put by the makers about their own product, in a blog post that says plainly they do not know the answer.
suggested_refs: Anthropic, 'Exploring model welfare,' 24 April 2025, built on a philosophers' report including David Chalmers
sources: Anthropic, 'Exploring model welfare' (anthropic.com/news/exploring-model-welfare)

stops.name: San Francisco, the thing is handed to everybody
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: released as a free research preview built on GPT-3.5, reaching roughly a hundred million monthly users within about two months. The link to the golem tradition is the compiler's; the release itself invokes nothing of the kind.
stops.campa: OpenAI puts a conversational model on the public internet as a research preview, and inside two months about a hundred million people a month are talking to it. The old questions arrive with the traffic, not one of them new and all of them now practical: whether the thing understands, whether it can be believed, whether the people who set it going answer for what it does. The number of human beings who have spoken with such a creature is now larger than the number who have heard the legend.
suggested_refs: John Searle's Chinese Room argument (Berkeley, 1980), which his own record applies to this release
sources: OpenAI release announcement, 30 November 2022
History.com, 'ChatGPT, the generative AI chatbot, is released'

stops.name: Mountain View, an engineer says it is a person
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month for the claim, the published transcripts, and the company's response. The link to the golem tradition is the compiler's: no participant in the episode is on record invoking it.
stops.campa: A Google engineer talks with a language model over months, concludes that it is sentient and ought to be treated as a person, and publishes edited conversations as his evidence. His employer reviews the claim, finds the evidence insufficient, and dismisses him. Rabbi Zeira needed a single unanswered question to know what he was dealing with; this thing answers everything, fluently, in whatever register is asked of it. Nobody involved on either side can name a test that would settle the matter.
suggested_refs: The edited LaMDA conversation transcripts published in June 2022

stops.name: Josefov, the creature on the menu
stops.date_confidence: Present-day observation; the date marks the state of the quarter at the time of writing rather than any event.
stops.campa: In the old Jewish quarter the golem is a restaurant, a beer, a puppet in a shop window, a marzipan figure, a walking tour that finishes under the Altneuschul with everyone looking up at the roof. The city's own tourist board keeps a page about him. None of the trade descends from the Talmud or from Worms; all of it descends from Rosenberg's invented manuscript by way of Wegener's film. The attic above the crowd has been searched at least three times and holds, so far as anyone has established, nothing at all.
suggested_refs: Prague City Tourism's official golem page; the restaurant U Golema and the golem walking tours of Josefov
sources: Prague City Tourism, 'The Golem of Prague'

stops.name: Venice, the negative comes back
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: pre-opening event of the 75th Venice Film Festival, Sala Darsena, with a commissioned score by Admir Shkurtaj played live. The Murnau-Stiftung describes the restoration as based on the original negative; the composite of four archival elements named in some accounts is not confirmed by any source read.
stops.campa: The 1920 film is restored in Bologna and shown on the Lido with a new score played live in the hall. Ninety-eight years after the Ufa-Palast, the clay body walks again at a resolution nobody in 1920 could have seen it in, in front of an audience that mostly knows the face from posters, tattoos, and every subsequent monster built on the same silhouette. The body that survived the century is the one made last, out of the three, by chance. The negative was long thought lost. The two earlier Wegener films are still missing.
suggested_refs: The Friedrich-Wilhelm-Murnau-Stiftung 4K restoration, carried out by L'Immagine Ritrovata, Bologna

stops.name: Prague, Vezenska, a bronze with no head
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month of installation. The golem reading is not the sculptor's stated referent, which is Kafka's 1912 story Description of a Struggle; the identification is a later guidebook and tourist accretion.
stops.campa: Jaroslav Rona's Kafka rides on the shoulders of an empty suit, a figure with no head and nothing inside the clothes. The reference the sculptor gives is Kafka's own story about a man carried through the streets on another man's back. Within a few years the guides walking tourists past it are calling the headless thing the golem, and the walk is sold under that name. Kafka never wrote a golem. He does not have to have; the city attaches the creature to whichever of its dead is currently the most famous.
suggested_refs: Jaroslav Rona's Kafka monument, Vezenska street, near the Spanish Synagogue
sources: Wikipedia, 'Statue of Franz Kafka'

stops.name: Krakow, Golem XIV stops talking to us
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year for the expanded Polish book; a partial form appears in Wielkosc urojona in 1973.
stops.campa: Stanislaw Lem writes the fictional documentation of a military computer built to plan wars. Lem gives it a serial number and the old name. The machine examines the assignment it was made for, declines it, and lectures its owners on evolution and intelligence instead, at length, in the register of a lecturer addressing a slower species. The golem of Chelm grew until its maker could no longer reach its forehead; this one grows in the same direction. Then it stops speaking to human beings, and the documentation ends.
suggested_refs: Wielkosc urojona (1973), where GOLEM XIV first appears in part
sources: Stanislaw Lem, Golem XIV (Krakow: Wydawnictwo Literackie, 1981)

stops.name: Cambridge, the program that is believed
stops.date_confidence: Attested for ELIZA: built at MIT between 1964 and 1966 and described in Communications of the ACM 9.1 (January 1966): 36-45. Placed in this sequence as a machine that answers; nothing in the sources has Weizenbaum invoking the golem, and the connection is the compiler's, not his.
stops.campa: Joseph Weizenbaum, born in Berlin in 1923 and out of Germany with his family by 1936, writes a few hundred lines that turn a typist's sentences back at her as questions. People who know exactly how it works sit down with it and confide in it. His own secretary asks him to leave the room. He spends the rest of his career alarmed by what he has found, which is that the appearance of understanding is enough, and that nobody has to be deceived about the mechanism to be moved by the result. Rava's creature failed because it would not answer.
stops.quote: It is important to note that this assumption is one made by the speaker... it has a crucial psychological utility in that it serves the speaker to maintain his sense of being heard and understood.
stops.quote_source: Joseph Weizenbaum, 'ELIZA, A Computer Program for the Study of Natural Language Communication Between Man and Machine,' Communications of the ACM 9:1 (January 1966), quoted via masswerk.at/elizabot
suggested_refs: A. M. Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence,' Mind LIX.236 (October 1950), which makes textual answering the test of an artificial mind
sources: Weizenbaum, Communications of the ACM 9.1 (January 1966): 36-45, DOI 10.1145/365153.365168

stops.name: Rehovot, Scholem hands over the machine
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day; the address is published in Commentary 41:1 (January 1966).
stops.campa: At the dedication Gershom Scholem, who has spent forty years reading the manuscripts this creature came out of, stands in front of an electronic computer named after it and makes the comparison out loud. The Prague golem was raised from the earth of Bohemia and worked in silence. This one is made of transistors, is fed on punched tape, and answers. The name was his suggestion in the first place. He asks a modest thing of it, and asks it of the builders in the same breath: develop peacefully and don't destroy the world. Shalom.
stops.quote: So I resign myself and say to the Golem and its creator: develop peacefully and don't destroy the world. Shalom.
stops.quote_source: Gershom Scholem, 'The Golem of Prague and the Golem of Rehovoth,' address at the Weizmann Institute, 17 June 1965, published Commentary 41:1 (January 1966). Wording rests on two agreeing secondary quotations; Commentary and the National Library of Israel blog both returned HTTP 403.
suggested_refs: The published text in Commentary 41:1 (January 1966)

stops.name: Cambridge, God and Golem, Inc.
stops.date_confidence: Contested year: the MIT Press text reproduced online carries a 1963 imprint and the preface is signed at Sandwich, New Hampshire, 30 August 1963, while MIT Press catalogues and the National Book Award record give 1964. Both circulate. The underlying lectures are Yale, January 1962, and a seminar at Royaumont near Paris in the summer of 1962.
stops.campa: Norbert Wiener, who spent a war building machines that aim at moving targets and correct their own errors, writes a short book about what it means to make a thing that learns. He takes the golem for his figure and the sorcerer's apprentice for his warning: the danger is not disobedience, it is obedience, a machine doing precisely what it was told by somebody who did not think through what he was asking for. The book wins a National Book Award. Wiener dies in Stockholm the same year.

stops.name: Rehovot, the machine is given the name
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day: WEIZAC is decommissioned and its successor begins operating on 29 December 1963. The machine is first called WEIZAC2 and renamed on Scholem's advice; the dedication address comes eighteen months later. Golem B, planned from 1967, runs from 1974, so the 1972 successor sometimes cited does not exist.
stops.campa: Israel's first computer is switched off on the same day its successor is switched on, and the successor is not given a technical acronym. It is called Golem. The people who built it, at an institute among the orange groves in a country five years older than the machine, have named their fastest instrument after a mute clay servant out of a Prague attic. It works in words of seventy-five bits: one for sign, ten for exponent, sixty-four for mantissa, wider than the American machines of its generation.
suggested_refs: WEIZAC, preserved in a glass case in the Weizmann Institute's computer sciences building

stops.name: Retiro, Maipu 994: the poem
stops.date_confidence: The Borges Center bibliography gives Davar no. 77, Buenos Aires, July 1958, pp. 3-5, and is preferred here; some secondary sources give August 1958 or 1959. The pin is the sixth-floor flat at Maipu 994 where Borges lived from 1944 to 1985, not Villa Devoto as one lens had it.
stops.campa: Borges publishes a poem that opens on Plato's claim in the Cratylus, that the name is the archetype of the thing, so that the rose is inside the letters of rose and the whole Nile inside the word Nile. From there it goes to a rabbi in Prague bent over a doll he means to teach the secrets of letters, time, and space. The creature is a failure. It sweeps the floor badly, it does not speak, it is a cat's imitation of a man. The poem ends by asking what God felt, looking at his rabbi in Prague.
stops.quote: (El cabalista que ofició de numen / a la vasta criatura apodó Golem; / estas verdades las refiere Scholem / en un docto lugar de su volumen.)
stops.quote_source: Jorge Luis Borges, 'El Golem,' first published in Davar no. 77 (Buenos Aires, July 1958), collected in El otro, el mismo (1964)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, filed among the imaginary beings
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year of the Manual de zoologia fantastica; the enlarged El libro de los seres imaginarios follows in 1967.
stops.campa: Borges and Margarita Guerrero put the golem into a bestiary, in among animals that were never anything but words. The entry carries the Talmudic material, the Prague material, the erasing of the letter, all of it accurate enough, all of it shelved beside the basilisk and the double. A creature whose entire claim is that somebody once raised one out of river mud is catalogued here, with sources, among the fauna of the mind. Ten years on the book is enlarged and reissued as El libro de los seres imaginarios.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the golem on the Yiddish stage
stops.date_confidence: Reported and unpinned. The IFT's staging of Leivick lives in Argentine Jewish theatrical memory, but no production register with dates, director, or cast was recovered. The date orders the segment and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: On Boulogne Sur Mer the Idisher Folks Teater plays to immigrants and to their Spanish-speaking children, a left-wing Yiddish house that will end up performing in both languages. Leivick's golem is remembered as one of the things staged there, the creature spoken in Yiddish, on a stage, in South America. Buenos Aires had by then a Yiddish theatre public large enough for the claim to raise no eyebrow in anybody who remembers the street. No program, no review, no register has been produced to confirm it.

stops.name: New York, Leivick's creature refuses
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year of publication. The Habima staging in Hebrew at Moscow follows in 1925, one source giving 25 December, and a Yiddish Moscow production in 1927.
stops.campa: H. Leivick, who was marched to Siberia in chains as a young Bundist and got out through Manchuria, writes the golem as a Yiddish dramatic poem on the Lower East Side. His creature is neither a tool nor a monster. It is a being brought into existence for a purpose it never asked for, awake enough to suffer, and the argument of the poem is with the man who made it. Habima stages it in Hebrew in Moscow four years later, a Yiddish production follows there, and the play goes out onto the interwar Yiddish stage.

stops.name: Prague, the attic that keeps being searched
stops.date_confidence: The date of Kisch's search is contested: 1920 in some accounts, 1915 with publication in 1924 in others, around 1910 in others again, and merely the beginning of the century in the tour literature. The later geophysical survey is given as March 1984 by one Spanish-language source that could not be fetched, and only as the 1980s elsewhere.
stops.campa: The Old-New Synagogue keeps a genizah under its roof, and the tradition says the deactivated body lies there beneath the discarded books. People keep going up. A reporter with the community's permission finds beams, rubble, an old chimney pipe, a dead bird, fungus, and a bat hanging. Every empty attic is absorbed as more evidence: the body was moved, or stolen in the last century, or the searchers looked in the wrong part of the roof. A Czech investigator brings geophysical equipment decades later and finds nothing. Roof repairs later still turn up nothing.
suggested_refs: The genizah of the Altneuschul, searched by Egon Erwin Kisch, by Ivan Mackerle with geophysical equipment, and again during roof maintenance around 2014

stops.name: Berlin, the Ufa-Palast am Zoo
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day of the premiere.
stops.campa: The third of Paul Wegener's golem films opens at the Ufa-Palast am Zoo and gives the creature the body it has kept ever since: heavy, clay-colored, wedge-haired, arms hanging, a face that gives away nothing. Hans Poelzig builds a Prague of leaning walls that no city has ever looked like, Marlene Moeschke makes the interiors, Karl Freund lights it. The 1915 film survives in fragments and the 1917 one is essentially lost, so this prequel, made last and standing first in the story, becomes the only one anybody sees.

stops.name: Vienna, Rosenberg in German without Rosenberg
stops.date_confidence: Der Prager Golem appears at Vienna across 1919 and 1920 in successive editions; the supposed Maharal letter of 1582 that Bloch publishes in 1923 is regarded as a further forgery.
stops.campa: Chayim Bloch turns Rosenberg's Hebrew into German and is not consistently forthcoming about where he got it. The blood-libel golem now enters European reading in a language that carries it, detached from the man who invented it ten years earlier and offered as folk material recovered. Each layer of forgery is presented as the discovery of an older layer underneath. The German edition goes through successive printings at Vienna across 1919 and 1920. Four years later Bloch produces a letter of the Maharal's, dated 1582, which is not the Maharal's.
suggested_refs: Chayim Bloch, Der Prager Golem (Vienna, 1919-20), and the 1923 letter

stops.name: Prague, Loew in stone at the city hall
stops.date_confidence: Commonly dated 1914-1917; 1917 is the completion year usually given. A cast of 1914 by the same sculptor is held separately at the Maisel Synagogue.
stops.campa: Ladislav Saloun carves the Maharal for the new city hall on Marianske namesti, three hundred and sixty centimeters of stone in its niche, about six meters with the pedestal. The figure is the historical rabbi, the jurist and schoolman, in his own robes. The reason a Christian municipality puts him on the front of its offices in 1917 is the legend fastened to him eighty years earlier by a German novelist. The creature appears nowhere in the sculpture.

stops.name: Leipzig, Meyrink's intermittent double
stops.date_confidence: Attested: serialized in Die Weissen Blaetter through 1913 and 1914, published as a book at Leipzig in 1915.
stops.campa: Gustav Meyrink's golem takes no orders and defends nobody. It appears in the ghetto every thirty-three years, a face at a window, a stranger in a room with no door, and the man it haunts cannot be certain it is not himself. Nothing is made in this book. Something recurs. It sells enormously, and it is the form in which the creature reaches readers with no connection to Prague or to Judaism at all, among them a boy in wartime Geneva teaching himself German with a dictionary and a copy of this novel.
suggested_refs: Borges's own account of Der Golem as the first novel he read entire in German, Geneva, c. 1916-1917

stops.name: Piotrkow, the manuscript that never existed
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year. Auction and bibliographic records give the imprint as Piotrkow; a competing strand of accounts gives Warsaw, and the discrepancy is not resolved.
stops.campa: Yehudah Yudl Rosenberg publishes a book he says he is merely copying out: a manuscript three centuries old, written by the Maharal's son-in-law, found in the imperial library at Metz. There is no manuscript and no son-in-law's memoir. There is Rosenberg, writing, and lifting plot machinery out of a Conan Doyle story he has read in Russian translation. What he composes is the version everybody now means by the legend: the creature raised to defend the Jews of Prague against the accusation of ritual murder, obedient, and put away when the danger passes.
suggested_refs: Curt Leviant's translation, The Golem and the Wondrous Deeds of the Maharal of Prague (Yale University Press, 2007)

stops.name: Prague, the Sippurim carry it out of the city
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year of the Sippurim volume containing Weisel's version.
stops.campa: Leopold Weisel's telling goes into the Sippurim, the cheap German-language anthology of Jewish tales that Wolf Pascheles sells out of Prague by the volume. This is the delivery system. A story that has been in print eleven years is now in households across Bohemia, Austria, and Germany. From here nobody has to be told who the golem is; the tale arrives already known, which is the condition legends are usually supposed to start out in. Pascheles keeps printing volumes, and the collection is reissued for decades in a book people buy for pleasure and give to their children.

stops.name: Prague, the legend printed as local speech
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year for both 1841 items. The titles circulate in corrupted form; Dekel and Gurley give Klutschak's as 'Das Golam [sic] des Rabbi Loew' and Philippson's simply as 'Der Golem'.
stops.campa: Franz Klutschak prints a golem of Rabbi Loew in a Prague magazine and presents it as a tale going around among the city's Jews. The same year Gustav Philippson runs one in a German Jewish weekly, and Abraham Tendlau puts one in a collection of old Jewish legends. Three appearances in twelve months, in three cities, every one of them describing the story as older than itself. Whether anybody in Josefov was telling it before 1836 is a question the printed record cannot answer, and no manuscript has ever surfaced to settle it.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Maharal is given the creature
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year. Long and almost universally called the first attribution of the golem to Loew; the Frankl notice of November 1836 in fact precedes it by a year, a priority established only in scholarship after 2009.
stops.campa: Berthold Auerbach, writing a historical novel about Spinoza, needs a Prague full of legends and hands the golem to Judah Loew. It is more than two centuries since Loew died. The novel is read, the pairing is repeated, and within four years the same pairing is being printed in Prague itself as something the local Jews are saying. For a hundred and seventy years this book is credited as the source of the attribution. Scholarship after 2009 gives the priority to a short notice printed in Vienna the year before it.

stops.name: Vienna, clay under the roof of the Altneuschul
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day of the issue. The venue is not the Sonntagsblaetter, which Frankl founded only in the 1840s; Dekel and Gurley identify it as a brief entry in the Oesterreichische Zeitschrift fuer Geschichts- und Staatskunde 92 (1836): 368.
stops.campa: A short entry in an Austrian historical journal, signed with initials, reports something kept under the roof of the oldest synagogue in Prague: a piece of trunk-like clay, in its primeval form and color, known by the name Golem. Nobody has been up to look. The notice is printed in Vienna about a building three hundred kilometers away, and it is the earliest datable moment at which the creature has an address. Everything the Prague tourist trade now sells stands on one paragraph in a magazine.
stops.quote: Under the roof of the oldest synagogue in Prague (Altneuschul) ... there is preserved, in its primeval form and color, a piece of trunk-like clay, which is known by the name Golem.

stops.name: Berlin, the golem in a romantic novel
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year of publication.
stops.campa: Achim von Arnim writes a golem into a German novel and changes its sex. The creature here is a made double of the heroine, a counterfeit woman who can be mistaken for the original, and the word on her forehead is a device of plot rather than a matter of law. From this point the story belongs as much to German letters as to any study house. The book is Isabella von Aegypten, printed at Berlin in 1812. Nothing rabbinic survives the crossing into it except the mechanism: earth, a name, a thing that walks.
suggested_refs: Isabella von Aegypten (Berlin, 1812), the bridge into German Romantic fantasies of artificial persons
sources: Achim von Arnim, Isabella von Aegypten (Berlin, 1812)

stops.name: Prague, the rabbi who is given one afterward
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day for the death. The stop exists for a negative finding: no work of Loew's own, and no sixteenth-, seventeenth- or eighteenth-century Prague source of any kind, connects him to a golem.
stops.campa: Judah Loew ben Bezalel dies in Prague, a formidable and much-printed rabbi with a large body of work on law, education, and exile. Not one line of it mentions making a man. No Prague source for the next two hundred years mentions it either: no chronicle, no communal register, no gravestone, no enemy. The Maharal goes into the old cemetery entirely innocent of the creature, and stays that way for as long as anyone in Prague is writing about him. The attachment is made elsewhere, in German, in print, in the eighteen-thirties.
suggested_refs: The Maharal's grave in the Old Jewish Cemetery, Prague
Ladislav Saloun's 1917 statue, which monumentalizes the later attribution
sources: YIVO Encyclopedia, 'Yehudah Leib ben Betsalel'
Gelbin, 'The Golem Returns'
Negative finding: absence of contemporary Prague attestation

stops.name: Altona, the son answers his father
stops.date_confidence: She'elat Ya'avetz is issued in volumes at Altona between 1739 and 1759; responsum 82 sits in volume two, of the 1759 printing. The date 1750 that circulates in some accounts is unsupported.
stops.campa: Jacob Emden returns to his father's question and sets the creature lower still. It has no knowledge. It performs because it has been built to perform, the way an animal is trained to perform, and understanding never enters at any point. Two generations of one rabbinic house have now argued the legal standing of a being their own forebear is said to have raised out of dirt. The responsum sits in the second volume of his She'elat Ya'avetz, printed at Altona. He carries the family story forward in it: the ancestor at Chelm, the thing that grew, the Name pulled off the forehead.
suggested_refs: She'elat Ya'avetz 2:82, and Emden's Megillat Sefer for the family tradition
sources: Jacob Emden, She'elat Ya'avetz, vol. 2, responsum 82 (Altona)
Jacob Emden, Megillat Sefer (Warsaw, 1896)

stops.name: Amsterdam, does it count toward ten
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the printing of Responsa Hakham Tzvi at Amsterdam in 1712; the responsum's own date of writing is not given in the sources reached.
stops.campa: Tzvi Hirsch Ashkenazi puts the creature to the only test his profession can administer. Ten men are required for certain prayers. Is a man made by a man one of the ten? He has a stake in the answer, since his own family holds that his ancestor at Chelm made one. He decides against it, and the reasoning is legal archaeology: Rabbi Zeira destroyed Rava's man and was never called to account for it, therefore that man was not a man, therefore this one may be dismissed from the quorum.
suggested_refs: Responsa Hakham Tzvi no. 93, the golem-minyan question
sources: Tzvi Hirsch Ashkenazi, Responsa Hakham Tzvi, no. 93 (Amsterdam, 1712)
Jewish Encyclopedia, 'Ashkenazi, Zebi Hirsch'

stops.name: Altdorf, the aleph erased
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the printing: Wagenseil's Sota appears at Altdorf in 1674. The events it reports are set in Poland and reach the page as hearsay at two removes.
stops.campa: A Christian Hebraist prints a letter from a correspondent, and the golem acquires the two features everyone now assumes it always had. There is a word on it, emet, truth, and the maker who wants it stopped removes the first letter to leave met, dead. And the shutdown goes wrong. In Arnold's version the creature has grown too tall to reach and comes down on the man who made it, killing him. In the tradition that descends through Emden, the Name is torn from its forehead and the falling clay only scratches his face. Nobody has reconciled the two endings.
stops.quote: When the Rabbi [Elijah of Chelm] saw that this creation of his hands grew larger and stronger because of the Name, which, written on parchment, was fastened to its forehead, he became afraid that the golem might cause havoc and destruction. Rabbi Elijah summoned enough courage and tore the parchment with the Name from his forehead. Then it collapsed like a clod of earth; but in falling, it damaged its master and scratched his face.
stops.quote_source: As quoted in Jeremy Dauber, 'Three Golems I Have Known,' SAPIR Journal 10 (Summer 2023), rendering the Emden tradition rather than Arnold's ending
suggested_refs: Christoph Arnold's letter in Wagenseil's Sota, earliest datable printed source for the emet and met motif
sources: Christoph Arnold, letter published in J. C. Wagenseil, Sota (Altdorf, 1674)
Gershom Scholem, 'The Idea of the Golem,' On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism, pp. 200-201
Jacob Emden, Megillat Sefer (Warsaw, 1896), p. 4
Jeremy Dauber, 'Three Golems I Have Known,' SAPIR Journal 10 (Summer 2023)

stops.name: Chelm, a maker with a name and a grave
stops.date_confidence: Elijah Ba'al Shem of Chelm is a documented rabbi who dies in 1583. The creation story attached to him is a family tradition first written down more than a century later, and is reported, not attested, for his lifetime.
stops.campa: Elijah ben Aaron Judah, called Ba'al Shem, master of the Name, dies at Chelm in 1583. He is a real man with a real grave and descendants who know exactly who he was. He is also the first person in the whole history of this thing to be named as its maker. Before him the makers are Rava, or two sages on a Friday, or an unattributed set of instructions out of the Rhineland. After him the story wants a maker's name, a town, and a household. The story that gives him one is written down by his own descendants, more than a hundred years after his death.
suggested_refs: The Chelm tradition as reported by his descendants Tzvi Hirsch Ashkenazi and Jacob Emden
sources: YIVO Encyclopedia, 'Golem'
Jewish Encyclopedia, 'Ashkenazi, Zebi Hirsch'
Jacob Emden, She'elat Ya'avetz 2:82, family tradition

stops.name: Safed, a life that is not a soul
stops.date_confidence: Reported: the 1548 dating follows standard Kabbalah scholarship on Cordovero's writing, and the pool carries no primary citation for it.
stops.campa: In Safed the question stops being how and becomes what. Moses Cordovero grants that a man may animate the thing he has made, then refuses to let the animation be a soul. There is nefesh, there is ruah, there is neshamah, and there is a fourth thing, hiyyut, a vitality that a human hand can pour into matter and that confers none of the other three. A golem on this account may move, work, and be a genuinely living body with none of the three human souls in it. Cordovero sets the distinction down in the Pardes Rimonim, among his chapters on the soul.
suggested_refs: Cordovero's distinction of hiyyut from nefesh, ruah and neshamah, the standard reference in later golem soul-status debates
sources: Moses Cordovero, Pardes Rimonim (1548)
Moshe Idel, Golem (1990)

stops.name: Rome, the letters turned inward
stops.date_confidence: Hayyei ha-Olam ha-Ba is dated 1280; no source located gives its place of composition. Abulafia is in Rome that year, detained four weeks by the Franciscans after going to confront the pope, and settles in Messina only from 1281, so the Sicilian attribution common in secondary accounts is anachronistic for this work.
stops.campa: Abraham Abulafia takes the same alphabet and points it the other way. The permutations are still recited and the names still combined, but there is no earth on the table and no body on the floor. The practitioner writes the letters, sounds them, governs his breath, watches them turn, and the thing that is supposed to change shape is the practitioner. Nothing is dug up, nothing is kneaded, nothing has to be walked backward afterward. The permutations that raise a mute servant out of clay are the permutations that, aimed inward, are meant to open a prophet. Which of the two uses came first, no source in the tradition says.
suggested_refs: Hayyei ha-Olam ha-Ba, British Library ms. Or. 10867
sources: Abraham Abulafia, Hayyei ha-Olam ha-Ba (1280)
British Library manuscript catalogue, Or. 10867
Moshe Idel, The Mystical Experience in Abraham Abulafia (1988)

stops.name: Worms, the recipe written down
stops.date_confidence: Attributed to the circle of Eleazar ben Judah of Worms, whose own dates are given as c. 1165/1176 to 1230/1238; the exact textual attribution within that circle is debated, and 1200 is an ordering date only.
stops.campa: Here, in a surviving text, someone finally writes down how it is done. Two men, or three, never one working alone. Virgin earth from a mountain where nobody has dug. Water that is still running. Knead it, shape a body, then walk around the body reciting the letters of the alphabet in their combinations, each combination assigned to the limb or organ it is meant to raise. To undo the work, walk the circle the other way and say everything backward. The German pietists set it out as a rite, with its own reversal built in from the start.
suggested_refs: Sodei Razayya and the Worms circle's Perush Sefer Yetzirah, the earliest surviving anthropoid-making procedure
sources: Sodei Razayya / Perush Sefer Yetzirah, circle of Eleazar of Worms
Gershom Scholem, 'The Idea of the Golem,' in On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism (1965)
Moshe Idel, Golem (1990)
Encyclopedia.com, 'Eleazar ben Judah of Worms'

stops.name: Barcelona, the commentary that keeps the older material
stops.date_confidence: Judah ben Barzillai is active in the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries; 1100 orders the segment and is not an attested date of composition.
stops.campa: In the Call of Barcelona a judge writes a long commentary on the Book of Formation, and his value to everyone downstream is that he is a hoarder. He copies in what earlier hands said, including traditions of creation by letters that a tidier author would have cut. Nothing in the book builds a body; it transmits the parts list. Between the philosopher at Sura who explained the gates and the Rhineland circles who will kneel over wet earth reciting them, the material passes through this manuscript. Later readers meet the older traditions in his copy of them.
suggested_refs: Judah ben Barzillai's Perush Sefer Yetzirah, a transmission point for creation traditions
sources: Judah ben Barzillai, Perush Sefer Yetzirah
Moshe Idel, Golem (SUNY Press, 1990), ch. 2
YIVO Encyclopedia, 'Golem'

stops.name: Baghdad, the Gaon defends the gates
stops.date_confidence: The Arabic commentary is conventionally dated 931 and the dating is reported rather than documented here. By that year the seat of the Sura academy had effectively moved to Baghdad, and both names are used for it in the sources.
stops.campa: Saadia ben Joseph, head of the academy of Sura, sets out in Arabic what the Book of Formation means by its two hundred and thirty-one gates: the letters paired every way they can be paired, and a world assembled out of the pairs. He defends the scheme and at once fences it. A man who combines letters is not doing what God did in making something out of nothing; he is working inside a creation already finished. Every later maker will use the technique he has just fenced. Saadia dies in 942, head of the academy, and the commentary goes on being copied.
suggested_refs: The 231 gates of Sefer Yetzirah, the combinatorial scheme Saadia's commentary defends
sources: Saadia Gaon, Commentary on Sefer Yetzirah (931)
Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Sefer Yetzirah'
Encyclopedia entries on Saadia Gaon, 882-942

segments.name: The Unformed Thing in the Book

stops.name: Sura, the calf eaten on Sabbath eve
stops.date_confidence: Same Talmudic page as the Rava story; the site of Sura is disputed among historical geographers and these coordinates are approximate.
stops.campa: On the same page, two sages spend every Sabbath eve on the laws of creation and produce a calf a third grown, which they eat. The made animal raises no question whatever. Nobody asks whether it may be slaughtered, whether it is meat, whether anything was in it to begin with. It is dinner. The trouble starts only when the thing assembled in the study house has a human shape and stands there, silent, in front of a rabbi who was not consulted. Both creatures come out of the same book and the same Friday study, and only one of them raises a question. The calf is eaten in honor of Shabbat.
stops.quote: Rav Ḥanina and Rav Oshaya would sit every Shabbat eve and engage in the study of Sefer Yetzira, and a third-born calf would be created for them, and they would eat it in honor of Shabbat.
stops.quote_source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b, Koren/Steinsaltz translation via Sefaria
suggested_refs: The companion creation story of Sanhedrin 65b, cited wherever Sefer Yetzirah is credited with making living things
sources: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b (Sefaria)

stops.name: Mahoza, Rava's man will not answer
stops.date_confidence: Rava heads the academy at Mahoza and dies in 352; the Talmud gives no date or place for the act itself, and the pin follows his documented seat.
stops.campa: Rava makes a man and sends him to Rabbi Zeira. Zeira speaks to it. The made thing does not speak back, and out of that silence Zeira reads its whole provenance: not born, made, and made by a colleague at that. Return to your dust, he tells it, and it goes. One unanswered question is the whole of the examination, and the page gives no sign that Rava is consulted about the outcome. Every feature the story will later acquire is missing here. No clay is described, no forehead, no word written or erased, no city, no rampage, no defense of anybody.
stops.quote: Rava created a man, a golem, using forces of sanctity. Rava sent his creation before Rabbi Zeira. Rabbi Zeira would speak to him but he would not reply. Rabbi Zeira said to him: You were created by one of the members of the group, one of the Sages. Return to your dust.
stops.quote_source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b, Koren/Steinsaltz translation via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Sanhedrin 65b, the base text of every later creation story
sources: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 65b (Sefaria, William Davidson translation)

stops.name: Pumbedita, Adam spends an hour as a golem
stops.date_confidence: Babylonian amoraic material, redacted later; the century and the academy of transmission are conventional. The text names no place for the teaching.
stops.campa: In the Babylonian academies the first man's first day is divided into twelve hours and counted out like a workshop schedule. Dust is gathered in the first hour. In the second the dust is worked into a shape with no definition to it, and the tradition has a name for that shape: golem. Only in the fourth hour is a soul cast into him; in the fifth he stands on his legs; in the sixth he begins naming the animals. So the golem is not a rival creature made in imitation of Adam. He is Adam, two hours early, before the soul arrives.
stops.quote: In the first hour of the day, his dust was gathered. In the second, an undefined figure was fashioned. In the third, his limbs were extended. In the fourth, a soul was cast into him.
stops.quote_source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 38b, Koren/Steinsaltz translation via Sefaria
suggested_refs: Sanhedrin 38b, the twelve-hour account of Adam's creation
sources: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 38b (Sefaria, William Davidson translation)

stops.name: Jerusalem, the word that appears once
stops.date_confidence: The composition and redaction of the Psalter cannot be dated; the negative year orders the file and asserts nothing. The Temple Mount pin marks the Psalter's liturgical center, not a place of authorship.
stops.campa: One word in the whole of scripture carries him, and it carries him only once. Psalm 139 sets it in the mouth of a man speaking to God about his own making: golmi, my unformed substance, the thing that is body before it is anything in particular. The verse does not leave the shapeless mass alone with itself. It puts a book beside it, and written in the book are the days that the unformed thing will have. Matter without form, and writing that gives it a life. In that form the word occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible.
stops.quote: Your eyes saw my unformed limbs; they were all recorded in Your book; in due time they were formed, to the very last one of them.
stops.quote_source: Psalm 139:16, Revised JPS 2023 Gender-Sensitive Edition, via Sefaria
suggested_refs: The sole biblical occurrence of golmi, Psalm 139:16, Strong's 1564
sources: Hebrew Bible, Psalm 139:16 (Masoretic text)
Sefaria, Psalms 139:16, Revised JPS 2023 translation

timeline_note: Retrocausal: this journey is told from its last body backward to its first word, so the subject is dated by its final stop (2026) and stands last in the atlas.
